brief: Prescription glasses starting at $95 including lenses, free home try-on of 5 frames. Anyone who wears glasses or just got a new prescription.

profile.business_summary: DTC prescription eyewear brand offering glasses starting at $95 including lenses, with a free 5-frame home try-on program.
stated_claims: Prescription glasses starting at $95 including lenses
profile.fulfillment_notes: Offers a free home try-on program where customers can test 5 frames before purchasing.

relevant_tags.why: Operates on a direct-to-consumer model with home try-on shipping.
Prescription glasses require custom lens crafting and frame selection tailored to the individual.
Glasses serve as a prominent face accessory and style choice adjacent to apparel.
Many professionals require glasses specifically for computer work or reading in office settings.

persona_conflicts.evidence: The 'free home try-on of 5 frames' followed by prescription fulfillment is inherently a multi-step, delayed process.

note_signals.why: Swiftcart is focused on high-frequency, impulse-friendly purchases, whereas prescription glasses are high-consideration and require a prescription.
Marlowe & Co. caters to older, lower-impulse affluent women who are highly likely to need prescription eyewear and appreciate quality messaging.
Strandlab's audience is highly motivated by personalization and quiz-based onboarding, which aligns well with frame selection and prescription customization.

profile.gate_reason: The product, pricing, and core offer are clearly defined, allowing us to align them with relevant lifestyle and apparel publishers.
missing_info: Shipping times and return policy details

config.advertiser_summary: DTC prescription eyewear brand offering glasses starting at $95 including lenses, with a free 5-frame home try-on program.

assumptions: No target CPA/ROAS or margin given; assumed 60% gross margin (typical for apparel). Give a target CPA to replace this.
Target CPA = 70% of max affordable CAC ($95 x 60% margin x 1.1 orders = $62.70).

pricing.rationale: Acquisition goal with no conversion history: pay per click. Max CPC = target CPA $43.89 x click-to-purchase rate (1.0%-3.5% for apparel). Clicks are observable without trusting a pixel, so both sides can verify billing.
pricing.tcpa_unlock: tCPA unlocks after conversion tracking is verified and 50 click-through conversions are recorded; until then Disco can't predict conversion rate for this brand.

budget.pacing: even daily pacing; pause a host if CPA > 2.0x target after 150 clicks

allocations.rationale: score 0.31 -> relative fit x1.40 on CTR/CVR; max bid $1.23 (break-even at target CPA), start at 70%
score 0.29 -> relative fit x1.35 on CTR/CVR; max bid $1.19 (break-even at target CPA), start at 70%

warnings: No budget given: recommending $1,270, the smallest budget that buys 300 clicks per host.
Budget too small for Cloudfoot: concentrating on fewer hosts.

phases.name: learning
phases.rule: bid = start bid per host (70% of break-even); pacing adjustment only
phases.why: stable bids so measured CTR/CVR aren't confounded by bid changes

phases.name: enhanced_cpc
phases.until: tCPA unlocks after conversion tracking is verified and 50 click-through conversions are recorded; until then Disco can't predict conversion rate for this brand.
phases.rule: bid = start bid x conversion_likelihood x pacing, clamped to [floor, max bid]
phases.why: spend more on shoppers who look likely to buy, never above break-even

phases.name: target_cpa
phases.rule: Disco bids automatically to hit $43.89 CPA
phases.why: only once Disco can predict this brand's conversion rate

adjustments.reason: Bid higher when the shopper looks like a high converter: their persona match for this campaign vs the host's average shopper (from the serve-time persona posterior).
Under-delivering vs the daily plan -> bid up a little; over-delivering -> bid down.

bid_strategy.rationale: Start below break-even and fixed so the first two weeks measure the hosts, not the bidder; then bid per shopper within a hard ceiling (max CPC = target CPA x CVR), so a single click can never cost more than it's expected to earn.
